Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Vignette:
# Aroha

Aroha had been a forensic analyst for eighteen years, the kind of meticulous professional who could reconstruct the sequence of a crime from fibres and bloodspatter, who built cases on evidence rather than assumption. She was respected at the laboratory—quiet, reliable, someone other analysts came to when they needed a second pair of eyes on a difficult sample. Her colleagues knew her as steady. They did not know that for the past seven months, she had been unable to enter the building without her hands shaking.

The morning of March 14th, her youngest brother Rangi had called her at work. He was in the city for the week, staying in a hotel downtown, and wanted to take her to lunch. Aroha had said yes—they were close, separated by only two years, and she had missed him. She'd left the lab at noon, driven to the hotel, and found him in the lobby. They'd embraced. He'd smelled like the cologne he always wore. She remembered his laugh as they walked toward the restaurant. She remembered the exact colour of the shirt he was wearing: a deep blue linen shirt she'd bought him for his birthday.

They were crossing the street. The light was green. Aroha was looking at Rangi, listening to him tell her about his daughter's school play. A delivery truck, its driver distracted, ran the red light at forty miles per hour. There was no moment of warning, no time to pull him back. Rangi was struck directly. The sound of the impact—a sound she could not adequately describe but which lived in her head now, a dull wet crack followed by the screech of brakes—had become the centre of her world.

What remained in her mind were not the seconds before or after, but three isolated moments, each vivid and motionless. The first: Rangi's face as he turned toward the sound of the engine, his expression still open, still mid-laugh. The second: the moment of contact, his body's sudden stillness against the truck's grille. The third: herself on the pavement, her hands on his chest, the blue linen shirt growing dark. These three pictures played in her mind without narrative, without the mercy of sequence or explanation. When they returned—and they returned constantly—they came with the sound: that crack, that screech. Her brain would produce the noise with perfect fidelity, as though the trauma were playing through speakers mounted inside her skull.

She had taken two weeks off work. Then she had tried to return. The laboratory smelled the same—the familiar chemical tang, the hum of the equipment, the cool white light. But walking through the doors meant entering a space where she was expected to be the person she had been, and that person no longer existed. She would stand at her desk, her colleagues speaking to her, and feel as though she were watching herself from outside her body. By the second day back, she called in sick. By the third week of absences, her supervisor had called her at home, voice gentle, asking if she needed more time. Aroha had said yes, not knowing if she would ever be ready.

The not-eating had begun without her deciding to do it. Food lost its taste. More than that, the act of eating felt like a betrayal—a small assertion that life was continuing, that she deserved nourishment, when Rangi was not eating, would never eat again. She had lost twelve pounds. Her husband Hemi had stopped commenting on the empty plates, but she could see the worry in the way he watched her at dinner, the way he'd begun leaving sandwiches on the counter, as though abundance might shame her into consumption.

Sleep was impossible. She would lie beside Hemi in the dark and feel the memories gathering, waiting for her to close her eyes. So she stayed awake instead, scrolling through her phone until three, four in the morning, keeping the house dark and quiet so the sounds in her head would not echo. She had come to believe that her life as it had been—the marriage, the career, the small satisfactions of competence and partnership—had been destroyed in that moment on the street. Nothing felt meaningful now. The cases on her desk at work, the careful reconstruction of evidence, the pursuit of justice: these things seemed like the preoccupations of someone living in a world that no longer existed. She had lost faith in the idea that the universe operated according to any logic at all. Rangi had been kind, had been loved, had had a daughter who needed him. And he had been erased by a moment of inattention from a stranger. People could not be trusted. Life could not be trusted.

It was Hemi who had finally insisted she see someone. He had made the appointment, written down the date, placed the reminder on her phone. Aroha had not wanted to come. But she had come, because staying as she was felt like dying very slowly, and because some small part of her—the part that had once been a good analyst, that had once believed in evidence and process—wondered if there was anything that could make sense of what had happened, or at least make it bearable enough to live alongside.
